SATOM 1.10.0

Adds Upgrade Flow for whole maintenance windows, three diagnostic tools, the bookmarks rail and Concept Map, alert routing with syslog and webhook delivery, issue-tracker tickets, and an external API for WAF exceptions.

👤 ForViewerOperatorAdministratorAdvanced user

Released: 2026-08-17 · All releases

In short#

One of the largest releases so far. Maintenance windows become one staged workflow (Upgrade Flow), backed by change requests that carry evidence for every appliance they cover. Three new diagnostic tools — a certificate inspector, a false-positive explainer and a transaction tracer — join the Tools menu. The console gains a bookmarks rail and a Concept Map, the Admin Console menu moves to a grouped side column, and alerts can now be routed per channel and sent to a SIEM, a signed webhook, chat tools or an issue tracker. External teams can file their own WAF exceptions through the API. A long list of fixes also removes about 790 false alerts a week.

What's new#

Maintenance windows: Upgrade Flow#

Automation → Upgrade Flow turns a maintenance window into one staged workflow: run the pre-flight on every appliance in the window in one sweep, raise a single change request that cites all of that evidence, export the combined customer impact, then execute. Each step existed before, but one device at a time, so upgrading sixty appliances meant walking the path sixty times and still ending up with a change document whose evidence covered one box.

  • Live progress per appliance. A change request now shows every appliance it covers and what has happened to it: pending, running, ok, failed — and interrupted for a device whose run was started and never finished. Progress counts appliances reported, not time elapsed.
  • Start now brings the approved change's action forward and lets the scheduler run it. It does not bypass the window: approval is re-checked when the action fires.
  • Batched rollouts (waves). Split a selection into waves, one change request per wave, each with its own window, approval and evidence, so you can watch the first group before approving the next. Appliances are grouped in name order, and windows follow each other with the gap you configure and never overlap.

Change requests: evidence for every appliance#

  • A change request now cites one pre-upgrade run per device it covers. Previously it could rest on the evidence of a single appliance even when it covered twenty.
  • The change request page lists each appliance with the run that covers it, and names the appliances that have no baseline.
  • The customer-impact spreadsheet is built from all the runs together, without counting a service twice and without merging two appliances that publish a policy with the same name.
  • The pre-upgrade scheduled action now does the full pre-flight — backup, health checks, maintenance permission and a baseline of every published service — and keeps it as evidence, exactly like the pre-upgrade on the appliance page.

Command line: reboot or upgrade a device by name#

For operators on SSH during a maintenance window when the web interface is not available, the command line can now reboot or upgrade an appliance by name. It only selects the one scheduled action that is already tied to an approved change request and runs it through the same approval check as the scheduler — it can never allow something the web console would refuse. When it refuses, it says exactly why: no such action, no change request, change not approved or its window closed, the action also targets other devices or the whole fleet, or more than one possible action.

The command line can also show a device's configuration from SATOM's own stored copy, by section, table or row, including older versions. It works when the appliance is unreachable or rebooting. An ambiguous section name is refused rather than guessed.

Three new diagnostic tools#

Open them from the header Tools menu.

  • Certificate inspector. Paste a certificate chain (or the output of a TLS connection test) or probe a live address and port. It shows the chain from the server certificate upwards and verifies every link by checking the signature, plus expiry, key size, signature hash, whether the hostname is covered, and whether a pasted private key matches. When the chain cannot be checked on this node, completeness is shown as unknown, not as incomplete.
  • False-positive explainer. Paste an attack-log entry (syslog, JSON or a raw HTTP request). It tells you which module blocked, which exception type addresses it, which fields scope it and the exact FortiWeb change — computed by the same engine as the exception panel. It lists what it could not place and what the entry does not contain, and decodes layered encodings in the payload. It has no save button on purpose: an exception is built from the entry as the device reported it, not from pasted text.
  • Transaction tracer. Sends the same request through the appliance and straight to the backend, and works out from the device's configuration what the appliance forwards in between (clearly labelled as derived). Comparing the two answers "is it the WAF or the application?" in one sentence, with per-step connection, TLS and first-byte timings, TLS details, and export as a command line or a HAR file.

Safety rules for the probes: GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are always allowed. Any request that changes data needs the new monitoring.probe_free permission and an explicit tick for that call. Inventory destinations are always available; any other address and port needs the same permission. Cloud metadata addresses are always refused. Every probe and trace, including refusals, is written to the audit log.

Bookmarks rail#

A collapsible bookmarks panel on the right of every page, like a browser sidebar: folders, nested groups that collapse, and a search box.

  • Three stores are always there — Favourites, Folders and Shared — plus an inventory view that lists the live fleet, so the panel is useful before you bookmark anything and new devices appear automatically. Starring or filing a device turns it into a bookmark.
  • Everything starts collapsed; SATOM remembers what you opened.
  • What you see depends on your own permissions, never on those of the person who shared a bookmark — sharing cannot hand anyone a device they may not see.
  • Sharing moves a bookmark to the team rather than copying it, and is recorded in the audit log. Each person files shared bookmarks in their own way; a shared bookmark you have not filed yet appears under Shared. The number of unfiled and hidden rows is always shown.
  • Grouping order is your own setting: Profile → Bookmarks — grouping order. Nest any order of Line, Zone, Department, Product, Network segment and Tag. Each dimension may appear once, and an empty order is refused. The default matches the previous layout, and the inventory view is named after your order.
  • The Product group shows the product's real name (FortiWeb, FortiADC, FortiAnalyzer, FortiAuthenticator) in a pill lightly tinted with your own banner colour.
  • A direct link to the device. Each device row — and the Host line on the appliance page — has an arrow that opens the appliance's own management page in a new tab, next to the name that opens SATOM's page. The link is always built from the current address, always uses HTTPS, and a device with no usable address keeps a dimmed arrow with the reason.

Concept Map#

A new Concept Map page shows every page of the console as a mind map — SATOM in the centre, one card per topic, every page inside its card and clickable. One search box matches a page's name, purpose, address and the words people type under pressure, such as "certificate", "rollback" or "who changed it". A list view shows the same set for reading and printing. It is linked from the footer of every page and reachable from all five ADOMs. Pages you are not allowed to open are not shown, and the page tells you how complete its own coverage is.

Alerting: per-channel routing and new delivery channels#

Until now alerts had a single on/off switch, and every finding — even the informational ones — went to email and to the in-app bell.

  • Each delivery channel now has its own minimum severity and its own set of alert families. Defaults match the previous behaviour exactly (bell and email on, every severity, every family), so nothing narrows on upgrade. Failures of the alert engine itself, and findings it does not recognise, always get through.
  • Settings → Email & Alerts gains a Delivery sinks table (on/off, minimum severity and the seven family boxes) and a Syslog collector block. Preview now also shows which channels would actually receive each alert.
  • Syslog / CEF feed to a FortiAnalyzer or SIEM, off by default, over UDP or TCP. It is a record, not a recipient: it has no cooldown and it also runs on the standby, so the history has no gaps.
  • Signed webhook, configured on Settings → Admin console → Alerts. One signed request per evaluation carrying every finding for that channel, with automatic retries for temporary errors only. Two formats: SATOM's own, and the simple text format Slack, Mattermost and Rocket.Chat accept. The signing secret is stored encrypted and never shown again; a blank field means "unchanged". Targets on your private network are allowed.
  • Integration hooks gain an alert fired event, with starter examples for Telegram, Slack and Teams that you own once saved. A new Integration hooks channel (off by default) feeds them. Hooks are counted as queued, not delivered, because a separate service runs them.
  • Config-drift alerts say who made the change. When a device's configuration changes, SATOM checks its own audit log for a write it made to that device in the relevant interval and names the author, time and client address. An unexplained change is reported as before and now states the interval searched. A new setting under Settings → Alerts chooses whether an attributed change is reported as informational (default), as a warning, or not at all.
  • A new Alerting & notification delivery reference document describes all of this, including how to verify the webhook signature.

Issue tracker tickets (Jira Cloud, OpenProject, Vikunja)#

Settings → Integrations gains a built-in ticketing connection. Raising the change ticket on a change request now opens a real ticket and writes its reference and link back onto the change — no custom script needed.

  • The ticket lists the appliances by name, the affected services, the stored pre-upgrade evidence, and the appliances that have none.
  • A change that already has a ticket reference is never given a second ticket, even after a double-click, a browser retry or a second operator.
  • Test connection checks the configured project, not just the credentials, and reports who it signed in as, whether the project is reachable, and how long it took.
  • Existing custom hooks keep working alongside it.

External API: WAF exceptions and FortiADC rules#

Security and application teams can now file their own FortiWeb WAF exceptions — and, when trusted, apply them — through the integration API, along with FortiADC rules.

  • Only exception types from SATOM's curated catalog can be written. The API cannot write arbitrary appliance configuration, and signature changes stay with operators.
  • Filing for approval and applying directly are separate token permissions, both of which must be granted explicitly. Existing tokens get neither. A token that may only file and asks to apply is told so rather than silently downgraded.
  • A token can only withdraw what it filed; retries do not create duplicates; and a token limited to certain applications is refused when the target protection profile is shared with policies outside its scope.
  • FortiADC rules cannot be deleted through the API, because SATOM cannot tell who created them.

Firmware lines: API versions and registry reconcile#

  • A new API versions page in each product's API hub compares what each firmware line (for example 7.6 and 8.0) actually serves, field by field, from evidence SATOM already collects. A command-line preflight tells you whether a payload would be understood on a line before you write it. One of its answers is unmeasured — "no evidence", which is never the same as "yes".
  • A new Registry reconcile page on both API hubs shows, per endpoint, what the fleet's appliances report: endpoints no live appliance serves (proposed for disabling), endpoints that differ between firmware lines (never proposed), and those that cannot be proven or swept. Approving a proposal disables the entry; the page warns first when every witness runs the same firmware line.
  • The user guide documents both pages, and the API manual covers them in two new sections.

Administration#

  • Settings → Languages. Choose which of SATOM's five languages users may pick. A withdrawn language disappears from the profile picker, from the change-document language choice and from browser language detection. English cannot be switched off. Withdrawing deletes nothing: users keep their choice (their profile explains it is not honoured right now) and translations stay, and the page shows how many users picked each language before you switch it off.
  • Classification catalogs (zones, lines, departments) are edited one value at a time. Each value shows how many appliances, combos and segments use it. Renaming a value moves everything that uses it. Removing a value still in use is refused until you choose to clear or move its references. Values in use but missing from the catalog are listed with a button to adopt them.
  • French and Italian change documents are now complete and available.

What changes for you#

  • The Admin Console menu is a side column grouped by theme: System, Access & Identity, Certificates & Trust, Monitoring & Alerts, Network & DNS, Fleet & Devices, User Interface and My Account. It starts fully collapsed, keeps one group open at a time, and remembers the open group per browser. A section reached from a link or after saving opens its group. The sections, their icons and their links are unchanged.
  • Admin Console panes use a single column — cards, tables and banners stack at full width instead of sitting side by side.
  • Hovering or focusing a bookmark row lights it in your own banner colour instead of grey.
  • The alert "dispatched" count now only counts findings a channel actually accepted, and only those start the cooldown. Widening a channel's filter takes effect immediately.
  • CEF events carry local time plus an exact timestamp, so collectors no longer file events at the wrong hour on installations not running UTC.
  • The change-ticket hook sends much more: the change reference, each appliance by name with product, management address and firmware, a pre-upgrade summary per appliance, the appliances without one, and an existing ticket reference so a repeat request updates the ticket. Long affected-policy lists are capped and say so, with the true total.
  • Upgrade Flow uses Administration → Change Types for its proposed title, reason and rollback, like the single change form, in the document language you choose. A disabled change type is reported up front. Waves now carry the reason, rollback and language, refuse an untitled plan, and always keep the wave number in the title.
  • Bookmark links must be http, https or a path starting with /. A stored link that does not qualify stays visible and explains why it is not clickable.
  • The upgrade scheduled action now requires an approved change request, as its description always said.

Fixed#

False alerts (about 790 a week)#

  • Config drift on devices that had not changed. Fields the appliance changes by itself — its clock, internal counters, list order — triggered a new version and an alert every hour. They are now ignored when deciding whether a configuration changed; the stored snapshot still keeps them.
  • "Host degraded — CPU load" on an idle node. The figure divided the host's load by the node's own cores. CPU is now measured for the node itself; the host's load is still shown, labelled as the host's.
  • "ALL backends down" for servers the appliance reported as up. A pool member with no health check configured is now shown as unverified (warning) rather than down.
  • Alerts counted as sent when the mail server refused them, which also silenced them for six hours. Only real deliveries count now, each failed channel is named, and a run that reaches nobody shows as failed on the Monitoring page.

Other fixes#

  • After an update, every page on a standby returned an error for hours while the update reported success. Updates now restore whatever the node was running and check it over HTTP, standby included.
  • An update now fails — instead of a page breaking afterwards — when a page links to something that does not exist.
  • Regex Lab names the engine that judged the pattern and points out where it can disagree with the appliance; patterns the appliance accepts were sometimes reported invalid.
  • Renaming a classification value no longer leaves appliances in "(no zone)", baselines with an empty scope, or a duplicate grid of combos. An old settings address that bypassed these protections was removed.
  • The "nothing was sent" warning on a change request now names both the tracker connection and hooks.
  • The API registry could serve the wrong address when an endpoint existed for two API versions.
  • Firmware was blank for most FortiWeb appliances; rediscovery now records it.
  • Rediscovery could not tell an empty list from an endpoint the firmware does not have, so broken entries stayed clickable in the API Explorer. An appliance with too many errors (over 25 %), evidence older than 45 days, or old-format snapshots can no longer count as evidence for the catalog.
  • The broken "interface" endpoint was retired. Provisioning now uses the working one, so Network interface finally has a field list, along with SNMP community, SNMP user, RADIUS, user group and syslog.
  • Field-catalog harvesting refuses a firmware line the device does not run, records the real harvest date, and says which kind of "empty" it found.
  • A translated change document came out empty once its language was complete.
  • The API manual described only 6 of its 13 routes and omitted three error codes integrators can receive; both the in-product and public copies are corrected.
  • The API versions page told you to run a command that does not exist.
  • The profile's About card showed the active ADOM's logo; it now shows the console's own emblem, with the version beside the name.

Under the hood#

  • Stored script links blocked in bookmarks. A team bookmark could hold a script link that ran in every colleague's browser. Links are now checked when saved and again when shown, including rows restored from a backup or replica.
  • Unauthenticated API calls get a JSON error, every applied exception leaves an audit record naming the token and its owner, and refused calls are recorded.
  • A boot-time database update had been silently skipping three columns; this can no longer happen unnoticed.
  • The user guide now has sections for Bookmarks, Concept Map, Upgrade Flow and Languages, and describes the grouped Settings menu.
